summary.en: OpenAI introduces BioBasicsBench, a 100-task benchmark measuring how well AI agents interpret raw experimental data and handle everyday wet-lab science.

text.en: Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. As part of that mission, we want to help scientists accelerate biological research—from understanding disease to developing new treatments. For AI agents to contribute, they need to reliably interpret the experimental evidence scientists work with every day in wet labs, where they run experiments with biological samples. Everyday wet-lab work involves failed experiments, ambiguous images and conflicting observations. Existing benchmarks are built around charts and images selected for scientific papers may miss this ambiguity and the troubleshooting it requires. That’s why we’re introducing BioBasicsBench, a new benchmark developed with Ligo, a biotech company focused on enzyme design, to measure how well agents handle routine wet-lab analysis.
text.th: Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. As part of that mission, we want to help scientists accelerate biological research—from understanding disease to developing new treatments. For AI agents to contribute, they need to reliably interpret the experimental evidence scientists work with every day in wet labs, where they run experiments with biological samples. Everyday wet-lab work involves failed experiments, ambiguous images and conflicting observations. Existing benchmarks are built around charts and images selected for scientific papers may miss this ambiguity and the troubleshooting it requires. That’s why we’re introducing BioBasicsBench, a new benchmark developed with Ligo, a biotech company focused on enzyme design, to measure how well agents handle routine wet-lab analysis.

text.en: The benchmark’s 100 tasks test whether agents can interpret raw experimental data, identify errors, and recognize when the evidence cannot support a conclusion. Getting these tasks right matters because misreading an image or overlooking a problem with the controls used to check an experiment’s results can lead scientists to draw the wrong conclusion and spend time on experiments that won’t help answer their question.

text.en: At the ‘xhigh’ setting, which allows more reasoning per task, GPT‑6 Astra earned an average of 66.7% of the available credit, compared with 43.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. The results show progress on routine lab analysis, with room for further improvements in interpreting images, checking controls and applying experimental context.

text.en: BioBasicsBench uses raw experimental evidence, from gel images and colony plates to microscopy and instrument readouts.
text.th: BioBasicsBench uses raw experimental evidence, from gel images and colony plates to microscopy and instrument readouts.

text.en: BioBasicsBench has 100 tasks across five areas of routine wet-lab work: protein methods, imaging and cytometry, quantification and assays, nucleic acid methods, and molecular cloning. Tasks range from simple requests, such as reading the molecular weight of a DNA sample in a gel, to detailed assay analysis, but all involve routine work that wet-lab scientists should be able to complete reliably.
text.th: BioBasicsBench has 100 tasks across five areas of routine wet-lab work: protein methods, imaging and cytometry, quantification and assays, nucleic acid methods, and molecular cloning. text.en: Scientists created the tasks using data from their own experiments, pairing each question with expert-written grading criteria. Each task underwent an internal review by a Ligo scientist who had not written it, an external review by a PhD-level scientist working in a wet lab, and a final internal review.

text.en: Agents return a structured answer with the requested conclusion, measurement or recommendation and, where required, supporting reasoning. Answers receive credit against individual rubric criteria, allowing the benchmark to distinguish a correct conclusion from a partially correct analysis. Most tasks test several skills together, including biological knowledge, interpretation of images and other data, error detection and protocol understanding.

text.en: The inputs preserve the forms of evidence scientists work with: gel and blot images, plate photographs, microscopy stacks, sequencing reads, plate-reader exports and videos of bench work. A task can include several kinds of data. Reference sheets, such as ladder charts and plasmid maps, support the interpretation of the experimental evidence.

text.en: We evaluated seven models on BioBasicsBench: GPT‑5.2, GPT‑5.4, GPT‑5.5, GPT‑5.6 Sol, GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6 Luna and GPT‑6 Astra. The evaluation covers 37 model and reasoning-effort settings, with five attempts on each of the 100 tasks per setting, for a total of 18,500 results.
text.th: We evaluated seven models on BioBasicsBench: GPT‑5.2, GPT‑5.4, GPT‑5.5, GPT‑5.6 Sol, GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6 Luna and GPT‑6 Astra. The evaluation covers 37 model and reasoning-effort settings, with five attempts on each of the 100 tasks per setting, for a total of 18,500 results.

text.en: We report mean reward: the average task score, expressed as a percentage of the available credit. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals calculated by resampling whole tasks, keeping the five attempts for each task together.

text.en: Mean reward versus average output tokens per task, shown on a logarithmic scale. Each point represents a tested reasoning-effort setting; lines connect those settings in order. text.en: Recognizing what the data can and cannot show
text.th: Recognizing what the data can and cannot show

text.en: A common trap in science is over-interpreting the data, especially given the nature of bias that occurs when testing a hypothesis. Astra demonstrated a better ability to discern the limit of what the data shows and not draw unwarranted conclusions.
text.th: A common trap in science is over-interpreting the data, especially given the nature of bias that occurs when testing a hypothesis. Astra demonstrated a better ability to discern the limit of what the data shows and not draw unwarranted conclusions.

text.en: In this example, GPT‑5.6 Sol classified cells as dead based on the signal from a dye used to detect dead cells. But the detector could also pick up light from a second dye, so brightness alone could not justify that conclusion. Astra recognized this ambiguity and called for better controls to separate the signals.

text.en: Scientific research is highly multimodal, requiring constant visual interpretation and decision making. Astra displayed a significant improvement at handling multimodal data which was given in the form of photos and videos, as well as raw outputs from sequencing, plate-reader assays, microscopy and flow cytometry.

Astra displayed a significant improvement at handling multimodal data which was given in the form of photos and videos, as well as raw outputs from sequencing, plate-reader assays, microscopy and flow cytometry.

text.en: At the most basic level, this improvement was noticeable through GPT‑6 Astra’s ability to pick up on finer detail from images taken during experiments and therefore draw more accurate conclusions as shown in this example. This task asked agents to draw conclusions from a DNA cloning experiment, where controls are essential. GPT‑5.6 Sol saw no colonies on the negative control plate and based its conclusions on that observation. GPT‑6 Astra noticed that the plate was labeled with the wrong antibiotic and correctly rejected it as a reliable control.

text.en: Discounting data that contradict its preferred interpretation
text.th: Discounting data that contradict its preferred interpretation

text.en: Astra discounts observations that contradict its preferred interpretation. It concludes that vacuoles, compartments inside cells, are generally darker than the surrounding cell, even though some appear lighter in the same image. Both appearances matter: changing the microscope’s focus can reverse the contrast, so the darker examples do not establish a general rule.

text.en: Accelerating biological research requires getting the everyday work right. BioBasicsBench makes that work a target for improvement: interpreting raw experimental data, checking controls and recognizing when a conclusion is not supported. Progress on these tasks could help scientists spend less time troubleshooting and more time deciding which experiments to pursue next. Tracking these capabilities will also help us understand their implications for biosafety and biosecurity.
